source_text: Συλλογισάμενος οὖν τά τε σοφίας ἀγαθά, καὶ τὰ ἀφροσύνης κακά, εἰκότως ἂν ἱκανῶς θαυμάζοιμι ἄνδρα τοιοῦτον, ὅς τις φερόμενος ἀλόγως· ἔπειτα ἑαυτοῦ λαβόμενος, εἰς τὸ δέον ἐπιστρέψει. Φρονήσεως γὰρ καὶ ἀφροσύνης πολὺ τὸ μέσον, διαφορὰ δὲ ἀμφοῖν τοσαύτη, ὅση περ ἡμέρας πρὸς νύκτα. Ἔοικε τοίνυν, ὁ μὲν ἀρετὴν ᾑρημένος, τρανῶς τε ἕκαστα καὶ ἄνω βλέποντι· τῆς τε ἑαυτοῦ πορείας, λαμπροτάτου φέγγους καιρῷ πεποιημένῳ· ὁ δ᾽ αὖ κακίᾳ ἐμπεπλεγμένος, καὶ πλάνῃ παντοίᾳ ὡς ἐν σκοτομήνῃ πλανωμένῳ, τυφλός τε ὢν τὴν πρόσοψιν, καὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ σκότους τῶν πραγμάτων ἀφῃρημένος. Τέλος δὲ ἐπινοήσας ἑκατέρου τῶν βίων τούτων ἐγὼ τὸ διάφορον, εὗρον οὐδέν, καὶ ὡς κοινωνὸν ἀφρόνων ἐμαυτὸν καταστήσας, τὰ τῆς ἀφροσύνης ἐπίχειρα δέξομαι. Τί γὰρ ἢ τῶν σοφισμάτων ἐκείνων ἀγαθόν, ἢ ποία ὄνησις τῶν πολλῶν λόγων, ὅπου γε τὰ φλυαρίας ῥεύματα, ὥσπερ ἐκ πηγῆς ὁρμᾶται τῆς ἀφροσύνης; Σοφῷ δὲ καὶ ἄφρονι κοινὸν οὐδέν, οὐ κατὰ ἀνθρώπων μνήμην, οὐ κατὰ Θεοῦ ἀμοιβήν. Τῶν δ᾽ ἐν ἀνθρώποις πραγμάτων, ἔτι ἄρχεσθαι δοκούντων, ἤδη τὸ τέλος ἐπιλαμβάνει ἁπάντων. Σοφὸς δὲ οὐδέποτε ἀσυνέτῳ τοῦ αὐτοῦ κοινωνεῖ τέλους. Ἐμίσησα τοίνυν καὶ τὸν σύμπαντά μου βίον, τὸν ἐν τοῖς ματαίοις ἀναλωθέντα, ὃν διήγαγον τοῖς περὶ γῆν πόνοις προστετηκώς. Ὡς γὰρ συνελόντι φάναι, πάντα μοι λυπηρῶς ἐκμεμόχθηται ὁρμῆς ἀλογίστου γενόμενα ποιήματα· καὶ διαδέξεταί τις αὐτὰ ἕτερος, εἴτε σοφός, εἴτε ἠλίθιος, τὰς ψυχρὰς τῶν ἐμῶν καμάτων ἐπικαρπίας. Ἀπολαβομένῳ δέ μοι ταῦτα καὶ ἀπορρίψαντι, κατεφάνη τὰ τῷ ὄντι ἀγαθὰ προκείμενα ἀνθρώπῳ, σοφίας τε γνῶσις, καὶ κτῆσις ἀνδρείας. Εἰ δέ τις τούτων μὲν οὐκ ἐφρόντισεν, ἑτέρων δὲ ἐπτόηται, ὁ τοιοῦτος εἵλετο μὲν πονηρὰ ἀντὶ ἀγαθῶν, μετῆλθε δὲ κακίαν ἀντὶ χρηστότητος, καὶ μόχθον ἀνθ᾽ ἡσυχίας, ταράχοις ποικίλοις περιελκόμενος, νύκτωρ τε καὶ μεθ᾽ ἡμέραν συνεχόμενος ἀεί, σώματός τε ἐπείγουσι καμάτοις, καὶ ψυχῆς φροντίσιν ἀδιαλείπτοις, σφαδαζούσης αὐτῷ τῆς καρδίας, ἀλλοκότων ἕνεκα πραγμάτων. Οὐ γὰρ τὸ τέλειον ἀγαθὸν περὶ βρῶσίν τε καὶ πόσιν ἱζάνει· εἰ καὶ μάλιστα ἐκ Θεοῦ ἀνθρώποις γίνονται αἱ τροφαί· οὐδὲν γὰρ τῶν πρὸς σωτηρίαν ἡμῖν δεδομένων ἔξω τῆς αὐτοῦ ὑπάρχει προνοίας. Ἀλλ᾽ ὁ μὲν ἀγαθὸς ἀνήρ, σοφίας ἐκ Θεοῦ τυχών, εὐφροσύνης ἔτυχεν οὐρανίου· ὁ δ᾽ αὖ πονηρός, θεηλάτοις ἐλαυνόμενος κακοῖς, πλεονεξίαν νοσῶν, πολλά τε ἀθροῖσαι σπουδάζει, καὶ τὸν ὑπὸ Θεοῦ τετιμημένον ἐναντίον τοῦ πάντων Δεσπότου ὀνειδίσαι σπεύδει, δῶρα προτείνων ἄχρηστα, δολερά τε ὁμοῦ καὶ μάταια τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἀθλίας ψυχῆς σπουδάσματα πεποιημένος.
thought_title: Wisdom, folly and the emptiness of toil
orientation: Solomon weighs wisdom against folly, comes to hate the toil spent on empty things, and finds the true goods in wisdom from God.
pass_a_gloss: Having reasoned together then the goods of wisdom and the evils of folly, I would fittingly sufficiently admire such a man, who, being borne along irrationally, then having taken hold of himself, will turn back to what is needful. For of prudence and folly much is the interval, and the difference of both is as great as that of day toward night. He then who has chosen virtue resembles one seeing each thing clearly and upward, and having made his own journey in the season of most brilliant light; but he in turn entangled in vice and in every kind of wandering resembles one wandering as in a moonless night, being blind as to sight, and deprived of things by the darkness. But having considered the difference of the end of each of these lives, I found nothing; and as having set myself a partner of the senseless, I shall receive the wages of folly. For what good is there either of those sophistries, or what sort of benefit of the many words, where indeed the streams of babble rush forth as from a spring of folly? But to wise and senseless nothing is common, neither according to the memory of men nor according to the repayment of God. Of the affairs among men, while they still seem to begin, the end already lays hold of all. But a wise man never shares the same end with an unintelligent one. I hated therefore also my whole life, the one consumed in vain things, which I passed through having melted onto, become attached to, the toils about the earth. For, to speak summing up, all things have been toiled out by me painfully, having become makings of an unreasoning impulse; and another will succeed to them, whether wise or stupid: the cold after-fruits of my labors. But to me, having taken these apart and having cast them away, there appeared the really good things set before a human being: knowledge of wisdom and possession of courage. But if anyone did not care for these, but has been fluttered, excited about others, such a one chose evil things instead of good, pursued vice instead of goodness, and toil instead of quiet, dragged around by varied disturbances, held fast always by night and by day, by pressing labors of body and unceasing cares of soul, his heart struggling convulsively for the sake of strange affairs. For the perfect good does not sit in eating and drinking, even if most of all from God the foods come to men; for nothing of the things given to us for preservation, safety, exists outside his providence. But the good man, having obtained wisdom from God, obtained heavenly gladness; but the wicked one, driven by God-sent evils, sick with greed, is eager to gather many things, and hastens to reproach the one honored by God before the Master of all, holding out useless gifts, having made deceitful and vain things the pursuits of his own wretched soul.

pass_b_english: So, weighing together the goods of wisdom and the evils of folly, I would rightly admire, and greatly, any man who has been carried along without reason and then takes hold of himself and turns back to what he ought (Ecclesiastes 2:12). For the gap between good sense and folly is wide; the difference between them is as great as between day and night (Ecclesiastes 2:13). The one who has chosen virtue is like a man who sees each thing clearly and looks upward, and who makes his journey in the brightest daylight; but the one entangled in wickedness is like a man straying in every kind of error, as on a moonless night, blind to what lies before him and cut off by the darkness from the things around him (Ecclesiastes 2:14).

Yet when I considered how the end of each of these two lives differs, I found no difference; and since I had made myself a companion of fools, I shall receive the wages of folly (Ecclesiastes 2:14-15). For what good is there in those clever arguments, or what profit in many words, when streams of idle talk pour out as from the spring of folly (Ecclesiastes 2:15)? Yet the wise man and the fool have nothing in common, neither in how people remember them nor in how God repays them (Ecclesiastes 2:16). Human affairs still seem to be beginning when their end already overtakes them all. But the wise man never shares the same end as the senseless.

So I came to hate my whole life, spent as it was on empty things, which I passed melting away over earthly toils (Ecclesiastes 2:17). For, in short, everything I labored over so painfully was the work of thoughtless impulse; and someone else will inherit it, whether wise or foolish, the cheerless fruit of my labors (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19). But when I had set these things aside and thrown them away, the goods truly set before a human being came into view: the knowledge of wisdom and the gaining of courage (Ecclesiastes 2:20-21).

But if someone has not cared for these, and has been swept away by other things, such a man has chosen evil instead of good, pursued wickedness instead of kindness, and toil instead of rest (Ecclesiastes 2:22). He is dragged about by troubles of every kind, held in their grip night and day without end, by the pressing labors of the body and the ceaseless cares of the soul, while his heart writhes within him over strange things (Ecclesiastes 2:23). For the perfect good does not rest in eating and drinking, even though food certainly comes to human beings from God (Ecclesiastes 2:24-25); for nothing given to us for our preservation lies outside His providence. But the good man, having received wisdom from God, has received heavenly joy; while the wicked man, driven by evils sent from God and sick with greed, is eager to heap up much, and hurries to cast reproach, before the Master of all, on the man whom God has honored, holding out useless gifts, having made deceitful and empty things the pursuits of his own wretched soul (Ecclesiastes 2:26).
notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 2:12-26. Doubtful (flagged in the source row): the sentence ἔοικε ... βλέποντι· τῆς τε ἑαυτοῦ πορείας ... πεποιημένῳ is elliptical in both prints; read as 'like one who sees ... and who makes his journey in the brightest daylight'. ὑπὸ τοῦ σκότους τῶν πραγμάτων ἀφῃρημένος is read as 'cut off by the darkness from the things around him'; 'robbed by the darkness of affairs' is possible. τέλος in 'when I considered how the end of each of these two lives differs' is taken as a noun ('end, outcome', matching Ecclesiastes 2:14b-15), not as the adverb 'finally', which would contradict the day-and-night contrast just drawn. Variant not adopted: the Opera omnia print (zoomed image at D) appears to read εὗρον ὥσπερ (or ὅσπερ) οὐδέν ('I found it as nothing'); sense unchanged. Τέλος could also be the adverb 'in the end' ('in the end, when I considered the difference between these two lives, I found none'); the noun reading is kept because Gregory's answer echoes it (τοῦ αὐτοῦ κοινωνεῖ τέλους). Gregory then corrects the speaker's conclusion: 'the wise man and the fool have nothing in common' and 'the wise man never shares the same end' answer Ecclesiastes 2:16 ('how does the wise man die? Just like the fool'); the last two sentences of that paragraph are his comment and are not cited. The 'courage' (ἀνδρεία) of the goods set before a human being follows the LXX of 2:21 (ἐν ἀνδρείᾳ). 'For our preservation' renders πρὸς σωτηρίαν, since the context is food that keeps us alive; 'for our salvation' is the other possible sense. The perfect good 'does not rest in eating and drinking' denies the plain sense of 2:24 ('there is nothing better than to eat and drink'); the citation is kept because the clause visibly answers that verse and 2:24b-25 ('this also is from the hand of God'). 'Melting away over earthly toils' keeps the image of προστετηκώς (melted onto, clinging to); 'heart' is not in the Greek. 'The cheerless fruit' renders ψυχράς ('cold', i.e. joyless). 'Master of all' renders Δεσπότης and refers to God.
